title: Bridging data and decision-making: A mathematical modelling perspective on infectious disease elimination
content:
by Emily S. Nightingale, Alexis Robert, Megan Auzenbergs, James M. Azam, C. Julián Villabona-Arenas, Han Fu, Katharine Sherratt, Sebastian Funk, Mark Jit, Katherine E. Atkins, Kathleen M. O’Reilly

Successful elimination strategies reduce transmission of a pathogen from stable and widespread endemic circulation to sporadic, localised outbreaks, paving the way for eradication when sustained across regions. However, the unique dynamics observed in pre-elimination and near-elimination settings create challenges for sustaining progress: observing sporadic cases, monitoring population immunity, and justifying continued investment in the context of growing complacency and competing priorities. For decades, mathematical modelling has informed elimination and eradication programmes by answering questions around the feasibility of elimination, the probability that transmission has been interrupted, and the risk of resurgence. This past decade has seen extraordinary technological advancement and momentous global change, both of which have had a profound impact on the status of these programmes. As new programmes are being established for some pathogens, long-standing candidates for elimination are facing local resurgences and threatening a return to pre-elimination dynamics. In this perspective, we present how novel data streams and methods may be leveraged by the modelling community to adapt to this evolving landscape. Specifically, we discuss three key areas for research that together shape the dynamics of elimination and resurgence: identifying the risk of travel-associated cases, evaluating the landscape of immunity and capturing the connectivity between social groups at highest infection risk. For each, we highlight priority research questions alongside recent advancements in data collection and modelling methodology that may serve to answer them. We conclude by emphasising the importance of active co-development with stakeholders across disciplines and geographic scales, to ensure that modelling insights are translated into local action and impact as well as global milestones.
author: Emily S. Nightingale
